role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Negotiation Starts With Your Walk-Away, Not Your Opening
summary: A negotiation is a search for a deal that beats what each side can get elsewhere. Before you open, you need three things written down: what you really need, what you will do if this deal fails, and the worst number you will accept. JAX joins Kema to show how a developer sets those before the first conversation.
body:
You do not win a negotiation in the room. You win it the evening before, when you write down what you will do if this deal fails and the worst terms you will accept, and then you refuse to change those numbers because someone across the table smiled.

Recall

Q. In a cross-border structure, what does a general anti-avoidance rule ask about a transaction?

A. Broadly, whether the main purpose was a tax benefit and whether the result defeats the purpose of the provisions relied on. The exact test differs by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What is the basic difference between selling a building as an asset and selling the company that owns it?

A. In an asset sale the buyer takes the property itself, usually with a fresh tax cost and with transfer taxes due. In a share sale the buyer takes the company, keeps its history and its tax cost, and transfer tax may differ. Each side prefers a different form, so the form is itself a negotiating point.

Q. Name the four usual ways to move money out of a project company to its owners.

A. Dividend, interest on a shareholder loan, a fee for services, or a return of capital. Each carries different tax and withholding consequences, so the choice is part of the structure, not an afterthought.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every development is a chain of negotiations: the landowner, the planner, the lender, the investor, the contractor, the buyer. A developer who negotiates well does not squeeze each party to the bone. He reaches deals that hold up under strain, because each side got something it needed and knows what it gave. A developer who negotiates badly either overpays because he fell in love with the site, or wins on paper and then spends three years fighting a counterparty who feels cheated.

This week JAX and I take negotiation apart: interests versus positions, the alternative you hold, the price you will not cross, anchoring and concessions. Today is the frame. The rest of the week puts money, law and a real room around it.

Positions are what people say; interests are why they say it

In plain English: a position is the demand on the table. An interest is the need underneath it. A landowner says, “I want 5,000,000 dollars, cash, in 60 days.” That is a position. Underneath it may be a tax bill due next spring, a family that wants to divide the money, or simple fear that a slow buyer will walk away.

The professional framing comes from Roger Fisher and William Ury, whose book Getting to Yes (1981) set out principled negotiation: separate the people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, invent options for mutual gain, and insist on objective criteria. It is not soft. It is a method for finding value that a pure price fight leaves on the table.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. You value a site at no more than 4,200,000 dollars. The owner demands 5,000,000 dollars in 60 days. You ask why 60 days. The answer is that he has a 1,000,000 dollar loan on the land that matures in 90 days and he cannot refinance it. That is his interest: certainty before the maturity, not the headline number. You offer 4,100,000 dollars, with a 1,000,000 dollar deposit released to him at day 45 to retire his loan, and closing at day 150 after your due diligence. He gets certainty; you get time. Neither of you moved off price as far as a straight haggle would have demanded.

Your alternative and your walk-away price

In plain English: the strength of your hand is what you can do if this deal dies. If you have another good site under option, you can walk. If this is the only site you have looked at in a year, you cannot, and the other side will feel it.

The professional terms are two. Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) is the specific thing you will do if no deal is reached: buy the other site, keep your capital in reserve, wait six months. Your reservation price is the worst number at which you still say yes, derived from that alternative. Write both down. A reservation price that is not written down drifts upward during the meeting.

Where the two sides’ reservation prices overlap, there is a zone of possible agreement (ZOPA): any deal inside it leaves both better off than walking. If your top is 4,200,000 dollars and the seller’s true bottom is 3,800,000 dollars, the zone runs from 3,800,000 to 4,200,000 dollars. Where the final number lands inside that zone is decided by information, patience and anchoring. If the seller’s bottom is 4,500,000 dollars, there is no zone, and the professional move is to say so politely and leave.

Say that out loud now.

A second worked example. You are offered two term sheets for the same building. Lender A will lend 20,000,000 dollars. Lender B will lend 19,000,000 dollars on lighter recourse. Your BATNA with Lender A is Lender B. That means Lender A cannot push you to accept full personal recourse unless the extra 1,000,000 dollars is worth more to you than limited exposure, and you have decided that in advance. The alternative you hold does more negotiating than anything you say.

Anchors and concessions

In plain English: the first serious number tends to pull the whole conversation toward it, and how you give ground tells the other side where your limit is.

You met anchoring in Week 3 as a bias. In negotiation it is a tool. A credible first offer, backed by a reason, anchors the range. An absurd one destroys trust. Concessions should get smaller as you go, each traded for something, never given for nothing. A pattern of 300,000, then 150,000, then 50,000 dollars says you are approaching your limit. A pattern of 50,000, then 300,000 dollars says you have no limit at all.

How the best do it

Institutional buyers that do many deals a year rarely let the deal team set its own price in the room. A committee approves a maximum price and the reasoning behind it before negotiation starts, and the negotiators need fresh approval to cross it. A small developer can copy this cheaply: write your reservation price and your alternative in a one-page note, sign and date it, and give a copy to someone you trust who will ask you why, if you want to exceed it.

Six-Lens Check

Tax. The form of a concession changes its tax character; a price cut, a deferred payment and a fee are taxed differently, so check with your adviser before trading one for another.

Liability. Statements of fact made to win a deal can become misrepresentation claims; bluff about your intentions if you must, never about facts.

Banking. Your lender’s term sheet sets an outer limit on what you can agree with the seller; never commit to a price your financing cannot carry.

Governance. Decide in writing who may make offers and who may sign, so that no one in your team can bind you in a hallway.

Estate. Long options and deferred payments outlast moods and sometimes people; make sure the agreements survive a death on either side.

Exit. Every negotiated term becomes part of what a future buyer or lender inherits; negotiate as if the next owner will read every clause.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is deal fever: wanting this site so much that your reservation price moves every time the other side pushes. The control is mechanical. Write the alternative and the walk-away number before the meeting, and require a written reason, given to a second person, before you exceed it.

The beginner's mistake

Treating negotiation as a fight over one number. Price is usually the least flexible term. Timing, deposits, conditions, who pays which cost and what happens if things go wrong are where both sides can gain, and the beginner never gets to them because he is still arguing about the headline.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal: from public information, work out the land price, rent and return that make a project work. That exercise is how you set a reservation price. Your walk-away number is not a feeling about the site. It is the residual land value at your required return, and you can defend it line by line.

Recap

Positions are demands; interests are needs, and trading on interests finds value a price fight misses. Your best alternative sets your strength, your reservation price sets your limit, and the overlap between two limits is the zone where a deal can happen. Anchor with a reason and shrink your concessions as you go.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: an auction where the winning bid became the loss.
checklist: I have written my best alternative to a negotiated agreement before the first meeting.
I have derived my reservation price from numbers, not from how much I like the site.
I have listed what I think the other side really needs, not just what they demand.
I know which terms besides price I can trade: timing, deposits, conditions, costs, risk.
I have planned my concessions to shrink, and each one is traded for something.
I have decided who in my team may make an offer and who may sign.
A second person holds a copy of my walk-away note and will ask me why before I exceed it.
Every statement of fact I plan to make is true and I can prove it.
head: Field checklist
speak: Negotiation is a search for a deal that beats what each side can get elsewhere. Positions are what people demand; interests are why they demand it, and the value is usually in the interests. Before I open, I write down my best alternative to a negotiated agreement, the specific thing I will do if this deal fails, and my reservation price, the worst terms I will still accept, worked out from the numbers rather than from how much I like the site. Where my limit overlaps the other side’s, there is a zone of possible agreement. If there is no overlap, I say so politely and leave. In the room I anchor with a credible number and a reason, I trade concessions rather than give them, and I make each one smaller than the last. I bluff about my intentions only if I must, and never about facts. And a second person holds my walk-away note, so I cannot quietly move it.
terms: BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) — the specific course you will take if no deal is reached, which sets how strong your hand is.
Reservation price — the worst price or terms at which you will still agree, derived from your best alternative.
Zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) — the range between the two sides’ reservation prices, inside which any deal leaves both better off than walking.

hostile.q: The landowner’s broker says three other buyers are ready at 5,000,000 dollars. Why should he take less from you?
hostile.a: If three buyers are ready at 5,000,000 dollars, he should take one of them, and I will wish him well. My number is 4,100,000 dollars because that is what the site is worth at the rents and costs we can prove, and I can show the arithmetic. What I can offer that others may not is certainty on his timing: a deposit released at day 45 to retire his loan, and a closing date I will commit to in writing. If those buyers turn out to need financing conditions, my offer stays open until Friday.

title: Stuyvesant Town: When the Auction Set the Price
summary: In 2006 a buyer won a famous Manhattan apartment auction with a record bid that depended on rents rising faster than law and the market allowed. By early 2010 the owners had defaulted and handed the property to their lenders. Ford and Roman trace how a negotiation without a fixed walk-away price became a loss.
rule: Rule 66: Write your reservation price and the assumptions that support it before any bidding begins, and walk away when the price crosses it; never let the auction set your number.
body:
In 2006 the winning bidder for Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village paid a record price that only worked if rents rose fast and the law allowed it. Neither happened, and by early 2010 the owners had defaulted. The lesson is about negotiation, not just leverage: the auction set the price, and no one’s walk-away held.

Recall

Q. When you defend a structure chart to an auditor, what is leakage?

A. The tax, withholding and cost lost each time money crosses a layer of the structure on its way to the owners. It is measured layer by layer, and a structure that cannot show its leakage cannot defend itself.

Q. What is recapture on the sale of a building?

A. Tax that claws back depreciation or capital cost allowance previously deducted, when the sale price shows the building did not lose that value. Rules and rates vary by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. Why does a treaty rate on withholding not apply automatically?

A. Because the recipient usually has to show it is resident in the treaty country and is the beneficial owner of the payment, often with forms filed in advance. Without that evidence the domestic rate applies.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this failure is told in two languages: the negotiation that set the price, and the debt that made the price fatal. Many people tell this story as a story about leverage, and it is. But underneath the leverage was a bid that no disciplined reservation price would have allowed. That part is what you can control.

The facts below are widely reported. Where I am not certain of a figure, I describe it without the number.

1. Timeline

Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village are neighbouring apartment complexes in Manhattan, with roughly 11,000 apartments, built by the insurer MetLife after the Second World War. In 2006 MetLife sold them through a competitive auction. A venture led by Tishman Speyer with BlackRock won at 5.4 billion dollars, then reported as the largest single residential property sale in American history. Most of the price was borrowed, with reserves set aside to cover the gap between the rent the buildings produced and the interest on the debt.

The plan depended on converting rent-stabilised apartments to market rents as tenants left. Through 2008 and 2009 the market fell and conversions came more slowly than planned. The reserves ran down. In late 2009 New York’s highest court ruled, in a case brought by tenants, that apartments in buildings receiving a particular property tax benefit could not be taken out of rent stabilisation in the way that had been done. In January 2010 the owners defaulted and handed the property over to their lenders. The equity, including money from public pension funds, was lost.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. First, the bidders entered a competitive auction for a unique trophy asset. Second, they bid a price that required rents to rise much faster than they had historically. Third, they financed that price mostly with debt, so the rent plan had no room to be late.

3. Assumptions

The price assumed that a large share of apartments would move to market rent within a few years, that Manhattan rents would keep rising, that the regulatory path to deregulation was secure, and that credit would remain available on similar terms for any refinancing. Each was plausible in 2006. Together they formed a single bet that everything would go right on time.

4. Incentives

An auction rewards the most optimistic bidder, not the most accurate one. This is the winner’s curse: when many bidders estimate the value of the same asset, the one who wins is usually the one who overestimated most. Fees for arranging, lending and managing were earned at closing, while losses would arrive years later and fall mostly on equity investors and junior lenders. A trophy also carries prestige, which is an incentive no spreadsheet shows.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

The rent growth required was far above the property’s own history. Tenant groups and housing advocates were vocal, which signalled political and legal risk around deregulation. The financing required reserves from day one to cover debt service, which meant the building did not support its debt on its actual income. A building that cannot pay its own interest on the day you buy it is not a stabilised asset; it is a forecast.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the bid itself, made with that capital structure. Once a price that high was financed that way, there was no lever left: rents could not be forced up faster, the reserves were finite, and the law was outside the owners’ control. Everything after closing was waiting to see whether the forecast came true.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a negotiation in which the price was set by the competition rather than by a fixed walk-away derived from defensible assumptions. A reservation price built only on the property’s proven income and a realistic, regulation-tested rent path would have been far below the winning bid. The discipline to lose the auction was missing.

Roman's view: how the debt turned a bad price into a total loss

Roman here. Overpaying with modest leverage gives you a poor return. Overpaying with heavy leverage gives you a deadline. A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. You buy a building for 100,000,000 dollars with 80,000,000 dollars of debt at 6 percent interest only, so interest is 4,800,000 dollars a year. The building earns 3,600,000 dollars of net operating income (NOI), so you fund a 1,200,000 dollar gap each year from a 4,000,000 dollar reserve. You have just over three years for the rent plan to work. If NOI rises 10 percent a year, it reaches about 4,800,000 dollars in year four, just after the reserve runs out. A delay of one year is fatal. Now imagine you had walked away from the auction at 80,000,000 dollars: the same rent plan, and the same debt ratio, would have covered its interest from the first day.

The lender’s question at underwriting should have been: does this building pay its own debt today? When the answer is no, the reserve is not a cushion; it is a countdown.

What a disciplined bidder would have done

Ford again. Discipline in an auction is not cleverness; it is a set of steps written down before the first round. First, value the property on the income it earns today, with no credit for plans that depend on a change in law or a change in tenants. Second, add the value of the plan separately, discounted for the chance it is late or blocked, so you can see how much of your bid is a bet. Third, set the walk-away as a single number, approved by someone who is not on the deal team. Fourth, decide in advance what you will do when you lose: the other properties you will pursue, so losing has a next step rather than a sting.

A worked example, hypothetical. A property earns enough to support a 70,000,000 dollar price on its current income. The value-add plan, if it arrives on time, is worth another 20,000,000 dollars. You judge a 50 percent chance it arrives on time, so the plan is worth about 10,000,000 dollars to you today. Your walk-away is about 80,000,000 dollars. When the bidding passes it, you stop, and you are glad to lose.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in any competitive process is that the other bidders’ optimism becomes your price. The control is Rule 66: fix your reservation price and its assumptions in writing before bidding, and walk away when the bidding passes it.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that winning the auction proves the price was right. In a crowded auction, winning is more often evidence that you were the most optimistic person in the room.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught stress tests: base, downside and severe cases, with break-evens and triggers. Run that test on this bid and the break-even rent growth is the whole story. If your deal only works in the base case and breaks in the downside, you are not negotiating a price; you are buying a lottery ticket with borrowed money.

Recap

A record auction price depended on fast rent growth and a deregulation path the courts later closed. Heavy debt and a finite reserve turned the forecast into a deadline, and the owners defaulted in early 2010. The root cause was a price set by the competition rather than by a written walk-away. Rule 66 fixes that.

Next: JAX on The Money: what each concession is really worth in dollars.
checklist: I have written my reservation price and its assumptions before the bidding opens.
My price works on the property’s proven income, not only on a forecast.
I have tested whether the building pays its own debt on day one.
I have checked regulatory and legal risk to any value-add plan.
I know the break-even rent growth and compared it with history.
I have asked whether winning would make me the most optimistic bidder.
I have agreed in advance who can approve a bid above my walk-away.
head: Field checklist
speak: In 2006 a venture led by Tishman Speyer and BlackRock won the auction for Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village in Manhattan at 5.4 billion dollars. The price depended on moving rent-stabilised apartments to market rents quickly, and most of it was borrowed, with reserves to cover the gap between rent and interest. The market fell, conversions slowed, and in late 2009 New York’s highest court ruled against the deregulation approach. In January 2010 the owners defaulted and the equity was lost. The forensic lesson is about negotiation. An auction rewards the most optimistic bidder, the winner’s curse, and here the competition set the price. A reservation price built on proven income and a realistic rent path would have lost the auction, which was the right outcome. Rule 66: write the walk-away and its assumptions before bidding, and walk when the price crosses it.
terms: Winner’s curse — the tendency for the winner of a competitive auction to be the bidder who most overestimated the asset’s value.
Rent stabilisation — a form of rent regulation that limits increases on covered apartments; its rules differ by place and must be checked locally.
Debt service reserve — cash set aside at closing to pay interest when the property’s income cannot.

hostile.q: Your bid is the highest by a wide margin. What do you know that the other bidders do not?
hostile.a: That is the right question, and if I cannot answer it with evidence I should not be the high bidder. My price rests on the income the property earns today plus a rent path I have tested against its own history and against the regulations that govern it. If my number is far above the others, I will go back and find which of my assumptions they rejected, and if I cannot defend it, I will lower my bid or withdraw.

title: Pricing Every Concession in Dollars
summary: A concession that feels small can be worth a lot, and one that feels big can cost you almost nothing. JAX shows how to convert timing, deposits and conditions into present-value dollars, so you trade what is cheap for you and valuable to the other side.
body:
Every term in a deal has a dollar value, whether or not anyone wrote it down. The developer who prices each concession before he offers it can trade what is cheap for him and valuable to the other side, and stop giving away terms that quietly cost more than a price cut.

Recall

Q. In a structure defence, what does a banker want to see that an auditor may not?

A. How cash reaches the lender’s borrower and where it can be trapped, delayed or taxed before debt is paid. The banker reads the chart for cash and control; the auditor reads it for substance and tax.

Q. Why does the choice between an asset sale and a share sale change the after-tax price?

A. Because tax cost, recapture and transfer taxes fall differently on each side. Two offers with the same headline can leave very different amounts after tax, so you compare them after tax, not before.

Q. What is leakage on repatriation?

A. The tax, withholding and cost lost as money moves from the project up to the owners. It is reduced by choosing the right channel and documenting it, not by hiding it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in Day 1 Kema showed that interests matter more than positions. Today we put prices on the interests. If a seller wants certainty and you want time, both of those have a value in dollars. When you know the value, you can offer the right thing. When you do not, you will either give away something precious or refuse something cheap out of habit.

The tool: present value of a term

In plain English: money paid later is worth less than money paid now, and risk you carry has a cost even if it never happens.

The professional framing uses two tools you already know. Present value, from Week 11, converts future cash into today’s dollars at a discount rate that reflects your cost of capital. Expected cost converts a risk into dollars: probability times the loss if it happens. Every concession can be priced with one of those two, and most with both.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A seller asks for 4,100,000 dollars all cash at closing. You propose 3,100,000 dollars at closing and 1,000,000 dollars twelve months later, with no interest. Your cost of capital is 10 percent a year. The deferred 1,000,000 dollars is worth 1,000,000 divided by 1.10, which is about 909,000 dollars today. So the deferral is worth about 91,000 dollars to you. If the seller would rather have a 75,000 dollar price cut than wait a year, offer the price cut: it costs you less than the deferral was worth to him. If the seller does not care about timing because he has no use for the cash for a year, ask for the deferral: it costs him little and is worth 91,000 dollars to you.

Pricing a risk you are asked to carry

In plain English: some concessions are not about timing but about who takes the hit if something goes wrong.

A second worked example. The seller wants your deposit to become non-refundable at day 30 instead of day 90. Your due diligence includes a geotechnical investigation that will not report until day 60. You judge, from past projects, that there is a 20 percent chance the report will reveal something that makes you walk. Your deposit is 200,000 dollars. The expected cost of making the deposit non-refundable before the report is 20 percent of 200,000 dollars, which is 40,000 dollars. If the seller offers a 75,000 dollar price reduction in exchange, the trade is worth considering, because it pays you more than the expected cost. If he offers 25,000 dollars, it is not. The probability is your judgment, not a fact, so write down how you arrived at it.

Say that out loud now.

Notice what this does in the room. You are no longer saying, “I do not like that.” You are saying, “That term is worth about 40,000 dollars to me; here is what I would accept for it.” That turns a fight into a trade, and it gives the other side a reason to keep moving.

Cheap for you, valuable to them

The best concessions are the ones where your cost is low and the other side’s value is high. Common examples in land deals: letting the seller stay on the land rent-free until construction starts; naming the building after the family; paying the seller’s legal fees; closing on a date that suits his tax year; or giving a right of first refusal on one unit. None of these changes your returns much, and each can matter a great deal to a particular seller.

The reverse is true too. Terms that feel minor to the other side can be expensive for you: a broad indemnity, an uncapped price adjustment, or a promise to start construction by a fixed date with a penalty. Price those before you agree to them.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick here. On your personal balance sheet, the most expensive concession you can make is your own guarantee, because it moves risk from the project to your household. A guarantee given to close a land deal or a loan may never be called, but it is a contingent liability: a debt that exists only if something goes wrong. Record every one, with its cap, trigger and end date. Price it like any other risk, probability times loss, and remember that the loss lands on assets you need for your family’s base. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Building a concession table

Before any serious negotiation, build a simple table with four columns: the term, its value to you, its likely value to the other side, and what you would want in exchange. Fill it in from the cheapest concession to the most expensive. In the room, you then move down the table, never up, and you always know what you are asking for in return.

A third worked example, hypothetical. The seller asks you to close 30 days earlier than planned. Closing early means you pay 30 extra days of interest on a 3,000,000 dollar land loan at 8 percent a year, which is about 3,000,000 times 0.08 times 30 divided by 365, roughly 20,000 dollars. If closing early lets the seller avoid a second year of property tax or a refinance, it may be worth far more to him than 20,000 dollars to you. That belongs near the top of your table: low cost, high value, worth trading for a price reduction or a longer deposit period. Write each line in dollars, with the assumption beside it, so you can explain any offer you make.

Keep the table private. It is your map of the room, not a document to share.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is giving away a term because it sounds small, when its expected cost is larger than the price cut you were fighting over. The control is to price every requested concession in dollars, present value or expected cost, before you answer.

The beginner's mistake

Only negotiating the headline price, and accepting every other term as standard. Standard terms are someone’s first draft, and each one has a value you have not counted.

Callback

In Week 38, JAX and Elias taught waterfalls and the tax character of developer fees. The same thinking applies here: a concession framed as a price cut, a fee or a deferred payment may be taxed differently, so the after-tax value of a trade is what counts. Check the tax character with your adviser before you swap one form for another.

Recap

Price timing with present value and risk with expected cost. Trade what is cheap for you and valuable to the other side, and refuse what is cheap to ask for and expensive to give. On your personal balance sheet, a guarantee is the most expensive concession of all.

Next: LEX on The Rules: what binds in a negotiation, and what you must never say.
checklist: I have priced every requested concession in present-value dollars or expected cost.
I know my discount rate and used it consistently.
I wrote down how I estimated each probability I used.
I have a list of terms that are cheap for me and valuable to this counterparty.
I have priced indemnities, penalties and deadlines before agreeing to them.
I checked the after-tax value of any trade between price, fee and deferred payment.
Every personal guarantee is recorded with its cap, trigger and end date.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every term in a deal has a dollar value, even if nobody wrote it down. I price timing with present value: a 1,000,000 dollar payment deferred a year, at a 10 percent cost of capital, is worth about 909,000 dollars today, so the deferral is worth about 91,000 dollars to me. I price risk with expected cost: if there is a 20 percent chance I walk after the geotechnical report, making a 200,000 dollar deposit non-refundable before it arrives costs me about 40,000 dollars. Then I trade. I give the things that are cheap for me and valuable to the other side, such as timing that suits the seller’s tax year, and I refuse the things that are cheap to ask for and expensive to give, such as broad indemnities. I check the after-tax value of any swap between price, fee or deferral. And I treat my personal guarantee as the most expensive concession of all.
terms: Present value — the value today of money to be paid or received later, found by discounting at your cost of capital.
Expected cost — the probability of a loss multiplied by its size, used to price a risk you are asked to carry.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes real only if a defined event happens, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: You keep putting dollar values on my client’s requests. Those probabilities are just your guesses. Why should we accept them?
hostile.a: They are my judgments, and I will show you how I made each one. You do not have to accept my numbers; you can tell me yours. What matters is that we are both pricing the same risk, so we can trade on it. If you think the chance of the geotechnical report killing the deal is lower than my 20 percent, then making the deposit non-refundable early costs you less, and you should be willing to give a bit more for it.

title: What Binds While You Negotiate
summary: Most negotiation happens before anyone signs, but that does not mean nothing binds. LEX explains when talks can create obligations, why a statement of fact made to win a deal can come back as a claim, and how settlement communications are protected. Law varies by place, so the concepts here must be checked against local law.
body:
A negotiation feels like talk until someone sues over it. Three things can bind you before the final agreement: promises in a letter of intent you thought was non-binding, false statements of fact made to close the deal, and terms you agreed so clearly that a court treats the contract as made.

Recall

Q. What is a mock interview at a checkpoint meant to test?

A. Whether you can explain a structure under pressure: accurately, in order, calmly, and with a direct answer to the hard question, not whether you can recite it.

Q. What is a departure tax, as a concept?

A. A tax some countries charge when a resident stops being resident, treating certain assets as if sold at that moment. Whether and how it applies depends on the country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What does a tax treaty usually do to withholding tax?

A. It may reduce the rate a source country charges on payments such as dividends and interest to residents of the other country, subject to conditions such as beneficial ownership.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers negotiate in emails, meetings and letters of intent long before lawyers draft a purchase agreement. If you do not know what binds, you can commit yourself by accident, or you can say something to win a point that becomes the basis of a claim years later. This lesson is concepts, not advice. Contract law varies by country and, in Canada, by province, and Quebec follows civil law. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it.

Agreement to agree, and subject to contract

In plain English: talks become a contract when the essential terms are agreed and the parties intended to be bound. Until then, they are just talks.

The professional framing: courts in common-law systems generally ask whether the parties reached agreement on the essential terms and whether they intended to create legal relations. An agreement to agree on price later is often not enforceable, because a key term is missing. Phrases such as subject to contract or subject to formal agreement signal that the parties do not intend to be bound until a final document is signed. Courts usually respect that, but not always; if both sides behave as if the deal is done, a court may find a contract anyway.

A worked example. You and a landowner exchange emails agreeing price, closing date, deposit and conditions. The last email says, “Agreed, see you at the lawyers.” Nobody wrote subject to contract. You then find a better site and stop responding. Depending on the jurisdiction, the owner may argue a binding contract was formed by email. The control is simple: put subject to contract in every negotiating message until you intend to be bound.

Letters of intent: the binding parts inside the non-binding letter

You met letters of intent in Week 20. The point to remember here is that most are mixed. The commercial terms are usually stated as non-binding, while specific clauses are expressly binding: confidentiality, exclusivity for a period, who pays costs, and governing law. Breaching an exclusivity clause by talking to another buyer can create liability even though the price was never binding.

Some jurisdictions also recognise duties of good faith in performing contracts. In Canada, the Supreme Court in Bhasin v Hrynew (2014) recognised good faith as an organising principle of contract law and a duty of honest performance. That case concerns performing contracts, not negotiating them, and its reach is still debated. Do not assume a general duty to negotiate in good faith exists where you operate; check locally [unverified — confirm independently].

Say that out loud now.

Misrepresentation: bluffing versus lying

In plain English: you may keep your limits to yourself, but you may not make up facts.

The professional framing is misrepresentation: a false statement of fact, made before a contract, that induces the other party to enter it. If proved, it can allow the other side to undo the contract or claim damages, and in serious cases it can be fraud. Statements of opinion, intention or negotiating posture are generally treated differently from statements of fact. “This is my final offer” is posture. “I have a signed offer from another landowner at 3,800,000 dollars” is a fact, and if it is false, it is dangerous.

A second worked example. To push a seller down, a developer says the city has told him the site will be rezoned for lower density. The city said no such thing. The seller sells cheaply. Later the seller learns the truth. That statement was a fact about the world, not a negotiating position, and it induced the sale. The seller may have a claim to set the sale aside or recover damages. A cheaper land price is not worth a lawsuit and a reputation for lying.

Without prejudice: talking about settling

When a dispute already exists, many common-law systems protect communications made in a genuine attempt to settle it, often labelled without prejudice. They generally cannot be used as admissions in court. The protection has limits and exceptions, and the label does not create it on its own; the communication must really be an attempt to settle an existing dispute. Ask your lawyer before relying on it.

Exclusivity and confidentiality in practice

A third worked example, hypothetical. Your letter of intent gives you 60 days of exclusivity: the owner agrees not to talk to other buyers while you do your due diligence. On day 40 his broker sends the site details to another developer. Even though the price in the letter is not binding, the exclusivity clause may be, and the owner may be liable for your wasted costs if a court finds a breach. Now turn it around. Your letter also says you will keep the owner’s information confidential. If you share his rent roll with a potential partner without permission, you may be the one in breach.

The practical controls are short. Read which clauses in any letter are stated to be binding before you sign. Track the exclusivity end date in your calendar. Keep a list of everyone who has received confidential information, and why. Ask your lawyer to make sure the binding clauses say what happens to deposits and costs if the deal does not proceed, because that is where disputes usually start.

What to put in writing

After every meaningful negotiation call, send a short note: what was discussed, what was offered, what remains open, and the words subject to contract. It costs five minutes and it is the best evidence you will ever have.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is making a false statement of fact to win a point, because it can unwind the deal and expose you personally. The control: before any meeting, list the facts you will state and the document that proves each one, and keep posture and fact separate in your own mind.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming nothing binds until the final contract. Exclusivity and confidentiality in a letter of intent bind now, emails can form contracts, and what you said to get there can be used against you.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to instruct professionals and keep records. Apply it here: keep a dated negotiation file with every offer, counter-offer and key statement. If a dispute arises about what was promised, the contemporaneous record decides it, not memory. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the governing law, before you sign any letter of intent.

Recap

Talks bind when essential terms are agreed and both sides intend to be bound, so write subject to contract until you mean it. Letters of intent usually contain binding clauses inside a non-binding letter. Bluff about your limits if you must, never about facts. Settlement communications may be protected, within limits.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: reverse engineering a closed land deal to find both sides’ walk-away prices.
checklist: Every negotiating email carries subject to contract until I intend to be bound.
I know which clauses in my letter of intent are binding now.
I have listed each fact I will state and the document that proves it.
I keep negotiating posture and statements of fact separate.
I keep a dated file of every offer, counter-offer and key statement.
I ask counsel before relying on any without prejudice protection.
A lawyer in the governing law reviews any letter of intent before I sign.
head: Field checklist
speak: Negotiation feels like talk, but three things can bind me before the final contract. First, if the essential terms are agreed and both sides seem to intend a deal, a court may find a contract, even from emails, so I write subject to contract until I mean to be bound. Second, letters of intent are usually mixed: the price is non-binding, but confidentiality, exclusivity and costs clauses often bind right away. Third, misrepresentation: a false statement of fact that induces a deal can let the other side undo it or claim damages. I may keep my limits to myself and say this is my final offer, which is posture. I may never invent a competing offer or a planning decision, which is a fact. Settlement talks in an existing dispute may be protected as without prejudice, within limits. All of this varies by place, so I check it with a lawyer before I rely on it.
terms: Subject to contract — wording that signals the parties do not intend to be bound until a final agreement is signed.
Misrepresentation — a false statement of fact made before a contract that induces the other party to enter it.
Without prejudice — a label for genuine settlement communications that, within limits, cannot be used as admissions in court.

hostile.q: In your email last month you told my client the city would not allow more than four storeys. That was not true. Why should the sale stand?
hostile.a: I take that seriously, and I will not argue it in a meeting. My recollection is that I said I expected the city to resist more height, which was my opinion, but you have the email and so do I. I will ask my lawyer to review the exchange with yours this week. If I stated something as fact that was not true, I will deal with it properly. I would rather fix it than defend it.

title: Reverse Engineering a Closed Land Deal
summary: Sage starts from a finished land deal and works backward to find your walk-away price, the seller’s likely walk-away price, the zone between them, and how much of that zone you captured. Every number is hypothetical and rounded.
body:
A closed deal is evidence. Work backward from the final terms and you can find your own walk-away price, a range for the seller’s, and how much of the space between them you actually captured. Do that after every deal and your next negotiation starts better informed.

Recall

Q. What is a reservation price, and where does it come from?

A. The worst terms at which you will still agree. It comes from your best alternative to a negotiated agreement, and for land it is usually the residual land value at your required return.

Q. In an exit, how do you compare an asset sale offer with a share sale offer?

A. Compute what each leaves you after tax, transfer costs and recapture, because headlines can be equal and net results very different.

Q. In a repatriation calculation, what is the first number to establish?

A. The cash actually available to distribute at the project level after debt service and reserves, before you calculate any tax or withholding on the way up.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most developers celebrate a closing and move on. The best treat each closing as a data point. What did I really pay, in present-value terms? How close was it to my limit? What does the seller’s behaviour tell me about his limit? Answering those questions builds a library of evidence about how much room there usually is, and that makes your next anchor and your next walk-away sharper. This is an even week, so we start from the finished outcome and work backward.

The finished outcome

All figures are hypothetical. You closed on a site for a headline price of 4,000,000 dollars: 3,000,000 dollars at closing and 1,000,000 dollars payable twelve months later, interest-free. The seller had earlier rejected a cash offer from you of 3,700,000 dollars. Your pro forma for the project shows stabilised net operating income (NOI) of 1,300,000 dollars a year and non-land costs, meaning hard, soft and finance costs, of 15,800,000 dollars. Your required yield on cost, the stabilised NOI divided by total project cost, is 6.5 percent. Your cost of capital is 10 percent a year.

Step 1: what did you really pay?

The headline price was 4,000,000 dollars, but part of it was deferred. Discount the deferred 1,000,000 dollars at 10 percent for one year: 1,000,000 divided by 1.10 is about 909,000 dollars. Add the 3,000,000 dollars paid at closing. The present-value price is about 3,909,000 dollars. That is the number to compare with your limit, not the headline.

Step 2: what was your walk-away price?

Work back from your required return. If NOI is 1,300,000 dollars and the yield on cost must be at least 6.5 percent, total project cost can be at most 1,300,000 divided by 0.065, which is 20,000,000 dollars. Subtract non-land costs of 15,800,000 dollars. The most you could pay for land and still hit your return is 4,200,000 dollars. That residual land value was your reservation price.

Check the result the other way. Total cost at the price you actually paid is 15,800,000 plus 3,909,000 dollars, which is about 19,709,000 dollars. Divide 1,300,000 by 19,709,000 and the yield on cost is about 6.6 percent. You cleared your hurdle by about one tenth of a percentage point.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: bracket the seller's walk-away price

You cannot see the seller’s limit, but his behaviour brackets it. He rejected 3,700,000 dollars in cash, so his reservation price was above 3,700,000 dollars, at least as he felt it then. He accepted a deal worth about 3,909,000 dollars in present value to you. If he discounts at a similar rate, his limit was at or below about 3,909,000 dollars. So his reservation price was somewhere between 3,700,000 and 3,909,000 dollars.

One caution. The seller may value the deferral differently. If he had no use for the money for a year, a deferred 1,000,000 dollars may have felt almost as good to him as cash, which means the deal felt like nearly 4,000,000 dollars on his side. That is exactly why the deferral was a good trade: it cost you less than it was worth to him.

Step 4: measure the zone and your share of it

The zone of possible agreement ran from the seller’s limit to yours. Take the conservative end of his bracket: from about 3,909,000 dollars up to 4,200,000 dollars, a zone of about 291,000 dollars that you kept. Take the other end: from 3,700,000 to 4,200,000 dollars, a zone of 500,000 dollars, of which you kept about 291,000 dollars and the seller about 209,000 dollars. On either reading, you captured more than half the available room.

A second worked example: what did the anchor do?

The seller opened at 5,000,000 dollars. You opened at 3,500,000 dollars. The midpoint of the two openings is 4,250,000 dollars, which is above your limit. Had you split the difference, as many people do by instinct, you would have broken your own hurdle. You avoided that because you traded timing for price instead of meeting in the middle. The lesson for next time: a high anchor from the other side makes the midpoint dangerous, so re-anchor on your own numbers and move the discussion to terms.

A third check: how sensitive is the answer?

Your conclusion depends on two assumptions, your cost of capital and your required yield on cost, so test both. At a 12 percent cost of capital, the deferred 1,000,000 dollars is worth about 893,000 dollars today, so the present-value price falls to about 3,893,000 dollars and the deferral looks even better. At 8 percent, it is worth about 926,000 dollars, and the price rises to about 3,926,000 dollars, still well inside your limit.

The yield hurdle matters more. If your lender or your investors insist on 7.0 percent instead of 6.5 percent, total cost can be at most 1,300,000 divided by 0.07, about 18,571,000 dollars. Subtract 15,800,000 dollars of non-land costs and the land limit falls to about 2,771,000 dollars. On that hurdle, the deal you closed fails by more than 1,100,000 dollars. A half-point change in the required return moved the walk-away by more than a quarter of the land price. That is why you fix the hurdle with your capital partners before you negotiate, not after.

Filing the result

Keep a one-page record for every deal you close or walk away from: your walk-away and how you derived it, the other side’s opening, every offer exchanged, the final present-value price, and the bracket you inferred for the other side’s limit. After five or six deals, patterns appear. You may find that sellers in one area usually settle about 15 percent below their opening, or that deferral is worth more to older owners than to younger ones. Those are your own reference classes, the outside view Kema taught in Week 2, and they are more useful than any rule of thumb from a book.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing headline prices instead of present values, which makes deferred payments look more expensive and cash deals look cheaper than they are. The control is to discount every payment to today before comparing it with your limit.

The beginner's mistake

Splitting the difference between two opening offers. The midpoint is set by whoever anchored more aggressively, not by the value of the site.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught yield on cost and the development spread. The walk-away price in this lesson is simply that idea run in reverse: fix the yield you need, then solve for the land price. If your market cap rate is 5.5 percent and your yield on cost is 6.6 percent, your development spread of about 1.1 points is your reward for taking construction and lease-up risk. Squeeze the land price and you widen it.

Recap

Discount the deferred payment to find the real price. Solve for the land value that just meets your required return to find your walk-away. Use the seller’s rejections and acceptances to bracket his. Measure the zone and your share of it, and file the result for next time.

Next: JAX on The Room: a landowner meeting where the first number decides the day.
checklist: I discount every deferred payment to present value before comparing offers.
I computed my walk-away land price from my required yield on cost.
I checked the closed price against my hurdle the other way round.
I recorded every offer the other side rejected and accepted.
I bracketed the other side’s reservation price from their behaviour.
I measured the zone of possible agreement and my share of it.
I filed the analysis so my next negotiation starts from evidence.
head: Field checklist
speak: A closed deal is evidence, so I work backward from it. Here, the headline price was 4,000,000 dollars, but 1,000,000 was deferred a year. At my 10 percent cost of capital that deferral is worth about 909,000 dollars today, so I really paid about 3,909,000 dollars. My walk-away came from the pro forma: NOI of 1,300,000 dollars at a 6.5 percent required yield on cost allows a total cost of 20,000,000 dollars, and after 15,800,000 dollars of non-land costs, land could be at most 4,200,000 dollars. The seller rejected 3,700,000 dollars in cash and accepted a deal worth about 3,909,000 dollars to me, so his limit sat between those two. I kept roughly 291,000 dollars of the room. And I avoided splitting the difference between the two openings, because that midpoint was above my limit.
terms: Residual land value — the most you can pay for land after subtracting all other project costs from the total cost your required return allows.
Yield on cost — stabilised net operating income divided by total project cost, the developer’s core return test.
Splitting the difference — settling at the midpoint of two offers, a habit that rewards whoever anchored more aggressively.

hostile.q: You paid 4,000,000 dollars for land you said was worth 4,200,000. Why should I believe you did not overpay?
hostile.a: Because the 4,000,000 dollars was a headline. One million of it is deferred a year at no interest, so at our 10 percent cost of capital the present value is about 3,909,000 dollars. On that basis the project yields about 6.6 percent on cost against our 6.5 percent hurdle. I can show you the pro forma behind the 4,200,000 dollar limit, and the earlier 3,700,000 dollar cash offer the seller rejected.

title: The Landowner Meeting: Holding Your Number Without Losing the Room
summary: A scene at a landowner’s kitchen table: an anchor of 5,000,000 dollars, a family with different needs, and a developer who must keep his walk-away price without making anyone feel squeezed. JAX gives the lines to say, the lines never to say and when to stay silent.
body:
In a landowner meeting, the number you hold matters less than how you hold it. Stay curious about their needs, calm about your limit, and quiet after you make an offer, and you can keep your walk-away price without losing the relationship.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause of the Stuyvesant Town loss, in negotiation terms?

A. The price was set by the competition in an auction rather than by a written walk-away based on proven income and a realistic rent path.

Q. In a meeting about an exit, why do you present the after-tax comparison rather than the headline offers?

A. Because the headlines can mislead; what matters to the owner is what each offer leaves after tax, transfer costs and recapture.

Q. When a banker asks why money is leaving the project as a fee rather than a dividend, what should you be ready to show?

A. The real service provided, the agreement behind it, how the fee was priced at arm’s length, and its tax treatment on both sides.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, land is often owned by people, not institutions: families, retired farmers, a widow who inherited a lot from her husband. They do not negotiate like funds. They care about fairness, respect, timing and what their neighbours will think. A developer who treats them as a spreadsheet loses sites to a buyer who listened. A developer who listens but forgets his number overpays. Today you practise both.

The scene

A Saturday morning at a kitchen table. The owner, in his seventies, has held the land for forty years. His daughter is there, and so is a neighbour who once sold land and now gives advice. Your written walk-away is 4,200,000 dollars, hypothetical. Your best alternative is another site under option at a similar price. The owner opens: “The land is worth 5,000,000 dollars. I am not giving it away.”

The question behind the question

When he says he is not giving it away, the question behind it is: will you respect what this land means, and will I be made a fool of? The daughter’s question, which she may not say, is: how quickly does this money arrive, and how is it shared? The neighbour’s question is: am I seen to be useful? Answer those questions and the number becomes easier to discuss.

The lines to say

Start with curiosity, not price. “Before we talk numbers, can you tell me what you want this sale to do for you and your family?” Then listen, and write down what you hear.

When you get to price, give your number with its reason. “My best price is 4,100,000 dollars. Here is how I got there: what we can build, what it costs, and what it will rent for. I am happy to leave this sheet with you.” A reason turns an anchor into evidence.

Then move to terms. “Is the timing of the money important to you? We could release part of the deposit early, or close on a date that suits your tax year. I would want your accountant’s advice on that.”

If they push, acknowledge and hold. “I understand 5,000,000 dollars feels right to you. I cannot get there and still build something the bank will finance. If someone can, you should take their offer.”

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never invent a competing site or a planning restriction to pressure them; that is a misrepresentation, as LEX taught on Day 4. Never say, “This is a fair price,” because fair is their word to decide, and you just told them what to feel. Never criticise the neighbour’s advice in front of the family. Never say “my final offer” unless it is, because once you move after saying it, every later number is doubted.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you state your number and its reason. The urge is to fill the silence with a justification or a small concession. Resist it. Count slowly to ten if you must. The next person to speak should be them. Stay silent, too, when the family talks among themselves; that conversation belongs to them, and interrupting it with a better offer teaches them that silence earns money.

Holding your state

A high anchor, a stubborn owner and a watching neighbour create pressure. Before the meeting, while parked, take a few minutes of slow breathing if that helps you settle, and remind yourself of your alternative. In the meeting, keep your voice even and your hands still. If you feel your number slipping, ask for a break: “Let me think about what you have said and come back to you on Tuesday.” A deferred answer is always available, and it is almost always better than a rushed concession.

A worked example of the trade

Over the hour you learn that the owner wants to keep living in the house for two years, and the daughter wants the money split into two payments for her own reasons. Price each. Letting him stay in the house costs you nothing until construction starts in month 18, then six months of delay to the part of the site under the house, which your schedule can absorb by building the other phase first. Splitting the payment into two halves a year apart is worth about 186,000 dollars to you at a 10 percent cost of capital on a 4,100,000 dollar price, because the second 2,050,000 dollar half is worth about 1,864,000 dollars today. You offer 4,150,000 dollars, two payments, and two years in the house. Your present-value price is about 3,964,000 dollars, well inside your limit, and each family member got the thing they cared about most.

Ethics thread: bluffing, honesty and inducements

This month’s thread is ethics. You may keep your limit private; you may not lie about facts. You may offer the neighbour your thanks; you may not pay him for persuading the owner, because a secret payment to someone advising the other side is a corrupt inducement in many places, whatever the amount.

Your reputation with landowners travels faster than your website. In a small market, the way you treated one family is how the next family will expect to be treated. Ask yourself after each meeting: would I be comfortable if every word I said today were read aloud to the next seller?

What you write after you leave

In the car, parked, write a short note before you drive: what the owner wants, what the daughter wants, what the neighbour wants, what you offered, what they said, and what you promised to send. Then send the family a short, warm letter by Monday: thank them for their time, restate your offer and its terms, and add subject to contract. That note protects you if memories differ, and it shows them you do what you say.

Then, at home, check every term you offered against your concession table and your walk-away note. If you went beyond either, write down why. If you cannot give a good reason, call back before the owner does and correct it politely. It is far easier to adjust an offer on Monday than to unwind a signed agreement in six months.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting the room move your number. The control is your written walk-away, your alternative, and the right to defer your answer to another day.

The beginner's mistake

Leading with price. The first ten minutes should be about their story and their needs, because that is where the trade that saves you money is hidden.

Callback

In Week 5, Kema taught pace and pause. Today you used the pause as a tool: silence after your number, and silence while the family talks. The skill is the same one you practised then; only the stakes are higher.

Recap

Begin with their needs. State your number with its reason, then move to terms. Never invent facts, never declare a price fair, and never pay someone advising the other side. Stay silent after your offer, and defer rather than concede under pressure.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 66 review.
checklist: I opened with the family’s needs before I discussed price.
I stated my number with its reasons and left the sheet behind.
I moved the discussion from price to terms.
I priced every term I offered in present-value dollars.
I stayed silent after my offer and while the family conferred.
I made no statement of fact I cannot prove.
I offered no payment or favour to anyone advising the other side.
I was prepared to defer my answer rather than concede under pressure.
head: Field checklist
speak: At a landowner’s table, I lead with their story, not my price. I ask what they want this sale to do for them and their family, and I write down the answers. When we reach price, I give my number with its reasons and leave the sheet behind, and then I move the talk to terms: timing, deposits, staying on the land, how the money arrives. I never invent a competing offer or a planning rule, I never tell them my price is fair, and I never pay someone who is advising them. After I make an offer I stay silent, and I stay silent while the family talks among themselves. If my number starts to slip, I ask for time and come back on Tuesday. In this case, two payments and two years in the house cost me little, kept the present-value price near 3,964,000 dollars, and gave each person what they cared about most.
terms: Question behind the question — the unstated concern that drives what someone says, such as respect, fairness or timing.
Inducement — a benefit offered to persuade someone; a secret one to a person advising the other side can be corrupt.
Deferred answer — a deliberate decision to respond later, used to avoid conceding under pressure.

hostile.q: The neighbour tells the owner, “He is lowballing you. Developers always make millions on these deals.” What do you say?
hostile.a: I would say: “That is a fair concern, and I would rather show you than argue. Here is what we expect to build, what it will cost, what the bank will lend and what we hope to earn. If we do well, it is because we take the risk of building and renting it, and that risk is real. You are welcome to have your own adviser check these numbers.” Then I would stop talking.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 66 Review: Interests, Alternatives, Limits and Concessions
summary: Six questions on negotiation, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a flawed negotiation brief, and a two-minute boardroom explanation. Answer each question aloud before you read the answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: decide your alternative and your limit before you meet anyone, then spend the meeting learning what the other side needs and trading terms, not haggling over a single number.

Recall

Q. How do you work out what a deferred payment is worth today?

A. Divide it by one plus your cost of capital for each year of delay. At 10 percent, 1,000,000 dollars a year away is worth about 909,000 dollars today.

Q. In a meeting about an exit, what usually decides which form of sale the owner prefers?

A. What each form leaves after tax and transfer costs, which depends on the owner’s tax position and is a question for a qualified adviser.

Q. What is the review question to ask about any repatriation channel?

A. What it leaves after tax and withholding, whether it is documented, and whether it matches the real substance of what happened.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, negotiation is the skill you will use most often as a developer, in almost every week of every project. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you are ready to sit with a landowner, a lender or a partner and keep your head. Answer each aloud first.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between a position and an interest?

Answer: A position is what someone demands. An interest is why they demand it, such as certainty, timing, tax or respect. Trading on interests finds value that a fight over positions leaves on the table.

Question 2. Define BATNA and reservation price, and say how they relate.

Answer: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement is what you will do if this deal fails. Your reservation price is the worst terms you will still accept, and it is derived from that alternative.

Question 3. What is the zone of possible agreement, and what do you do when there is none?

Answer: The overlap between the two sides’ reservation prices. If there is no overlap, you say so politely and leave.

Question 4. How do you price a request to make your deposit non-refundable early?

Answer: Expected cost: the chance you will want to walk before the risk is known, multiplied by the deposit. At 20 percent on 200,000 dollars, about 40,000 dollars.

Question 5. What is the difference between bluffing and misrepresentation?

Answer: Bluffing concerns your intentions or limits, such as calling an offer final. Misrepresentation is a false statement of fact that induces a deal, such as an invented competing offer, and it can unwind the deal or create a claim.

Question 6. Why is splitting the difference dangerous?

Answer: Because the midpoint is set by whoever anchored more aggressively, not by value, and it can land above your limit.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Kema and JAX set the frame: interests, alternatives, limits, anchors and shrinking concessions. Ford and Roman took Stuyvesant Town, where an auction set the price and heavy debt turned a forecast into a deadline, giving Rule 66. JAX priced concessions in present-value and expected-cost dollars. LEX showed what binds before signing. Sage reverse engineered a closed land deal. JAX ran the landowner meeting.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical negotiation brief, written by a junior team member, and find the defects before reading on.

Negotiation brief, Site 7. Our target is to get the site. Seller is asking 5,000,000 dollars; we should aim to meet him halfway from our opening of 3,500,000, so around 4,250,000. If he hesitates, tell him the city is planning a road widening that will take part of the frontage, which should bring him down. Deposit can go non-refundable at day 30 as he wants, since it is only 200,000 dollars. Our walk-away is whatever the investors will accept. JAX to negotiate; anyone in the team can confirm terms by email.

The defects. First, the target is getting the site, not getting it at the right price; a goal of winning invites the winner’s curse. Second, it plans to split the difference, and the midpoint of 4,250,000 dollars sits above the 4,200,000 dollar residual limit from our pro forma. Third, it proposes stating a road widening as fact with no evidence, which is a misrepresentation if untrue. Fourth, it gives away the non-refundable deposit without pricing it before the geotechnical report. Fifth, the walk-away is undefined and outsourced to investors rather than derived from numbers. Sixth, it lets anyone confirm terms by email, which can bind us without subject to contract and without authority.

Now rewrite the brief in your head: a defined alternative, a residual-value limit, a list of the seller’s likely interests, priced concessions, true facts only, and one named person with authority.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, “How do you avoid overpaying for land?” Then compare with this model.

Model answer: “Before I meet a seller I write down two things: what I will do if this deal fails, and the most I will pay. The most I will pay is not a feeling; it is the residual land value at our required yield on cost, so I can show the arithmetic. In the meeting I spend the first part learning what the seller needs, because the best trades are on timing, deposits and conditions, not price. I price every term in present-value or expected-cost dollars, I never state a fact I cannot prove, and I never split the difference from his anchor. If his limit is above mine, I leave and buy the alternative. After closing, I work backward from the deal to see how much of the room we captured, so the next one starts better.”

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the alternative and derive the limit? Did you mention terms beyond price? Did you finish in two minutes?

The corrected brief

Here is the brief as it should read. “Negotiation brief, Site 7. Goal: acquire the site at or below a present-value price of 4,200,000 dollars, the residual land value at our 6.5 percent required yield on cost. Alternative: proceed with the site under option on Elm Road. Seller’s likely interests: certainty before his loan matures, timing that suits his tax year, and remaining in the house. Opening offer: 3,700,000 dollars with reasons on one page. Concessions, in order: early partial deposit release, closing date of his choice, two payments, occupancy until construction. Deposit becomes non-refundable only after the geotechnical report, or for a price reduction of at least 40,000 dollars. Only verified facts will be stated. JAX negotiates; only JAX may confirm terms, in writing, subject to contract.”

Notice that every line can be checked. That is the test of a good brief: a stranger could read it and know exactly what we will and will not do.

Then do one more pass, as the seller’s lawyer would. Which line could he use against us later? In the corrected brief, none: there is no statement of fact we cannot prove, no promise made without authority, and no deadline we have not priced. That is the standard to hold every brief to before it leaves your desk.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is moving your limit under pressure. The control is the written walk-away, a second person who holds it, and the right to defer your answer.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising the vocabulary and walking into the meeting without having written down the alternative and the number.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema and Ford taught the pre-mortem: imagine the decision has failed and ask why. Before any big negotiation, run one: imagine you overpaid and ask what made you do it. The answer is usually a moved limit, and that is exactly what this week’s controls prevent.

Recap

Interests over positions, alternatives before offers, limits from numbers, concessions priced and shrinking, facts always true. Rule 66 protects you in an auction.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about negotiation. A position is what someone demands and an interest is why, and the value is usually in the interests. Before I meet anyone, I write down my best alternative to a negotiated agreement and my reservation price, derived from the numbers, usually the residual land value at my required return. Where my limit overlaps the other side’s there is a zone of possible agreement; where it does not, I leave. I anchor with a reason, I shrink my concessions, and I price every term in dollars: present value for timing, expected cost for risk. I keep my limits private but I never state a false fact, because misrepresentation can unwind a deal. I never split the difference from someone else’s anchor. Rule 66 says to write my walk-away before an auction and leave when the bidding passes it. And after closing I work backward to see how much of the room I kept.
terms: Pre-mortem — imagining a decision has already failed and asking why, before you make it.
Anchor — the first serious number in a negotiation, which pulls later offers toward it.
Authority to bind — the defined right of a named person to make offers or agree terms on your behalf.

hostile.q: Your investors ask: in your last three land deals, how close did you come to your walk-away price, and how do you know?
hostile.a: I can show you. For each deal I recorded my walk-away from the pro forma before negotiating, every offer exchanged, and the present value of the final terms. Then I bracketed the seller’s limit from what he rejected and accepted. On the most recent one we paid about 3,909,000 dollars in present value against a 4,200,000 dollar limit. I will send you the file for all three.
